(Oct 13): Copper and aluminium retreated as investor angst around overheated spending on artificial-intelligence infrastructure fuelled uncertainty about the demand outlook for the metals.

AI and technology stocks dropped across global markets following warnings the rapid buildout of data centres will become more difficult to finance. South Korea’s equity benchmark — which has been correlated with copper prices at times this year — slumped as much as 7%.

Copper bulls argue that AI infrastructure will be a key source of demand in the coming decade and any doubts about the pace of spending can hit trading sentiment. Still, the major driver for the red metal’s 17% rally this year has been the threat of US import tariffs, which has pulled huge volumes into the country and cut availability elsewhere.

“While not acting as the sole rationale behind the copper price performance in 2026 thus far, AI-driven sentiment is expected to continue to shape, if not dominate, the narrative in the coming years,” BMI, a Fitch Solutions company, said in a note.

Copper fell 0.2% to US$14,588 a tonne on the London Metal Exchange as of 11.25am in Shanghai (same time as Malaysia). Aluminium, which is also used in AI infrastructure, dropped 0.3% and zinc lost 0.7%. Iron ore declined 0.3% to US$90.70 a tonne in Singapore, touching the lowest level in two years.

KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 13): Deputy Energy Transition and Water Transformation Minister Datuk Seri Abdul Rahman Mohamad is proposing the government require data centre operators to generate their own electricity as part of a review of the sector’s energy and water consumption,

The Energy Commission (ST) is studying the actual electricity needs of data centres, following a gap between their contracted maximum load and actual consumption.

As at August 2026, 45 of the 62 data centres that had signed electricity supply agreements had begun operations. The operational facilities had a combined maximum load of six gigawatts (GW), but their actual electricity consumption stood at about 1.37GW.

Abdul Rahman said he had proposed that operators develop their own power generation facilities, allowing them to choose energy sources such as solar power and battery storage.

The government is also considering requiring data centres near ponds or other water sources to develop their own water supply systems for on-site use, to prevent them from affecting water availability for other consumers.

He said the ministry was examining the sector’s actual resource needs and whether some data centres would bring meaningful benefits to the country.

Meanwhile, the government is accelerating renewable energy development, targeting renewable sources to account for 35% of installed capacity by 2030 and 70% by 2050.

As at Sept 1, 2026, renewable energy accounted for nearly 32% of Malaysia’s installed capacity, or about 14,000MW. Another 10,000MW to 11,000MW of renewable energy capacity is expected to come online by 2030, based on announced programmes and private-sector plans.

stories.summary_zh: 据路透社看到的一份 IDC 报告，2026 年上半年 Nvidia 在中国数据中心 AI 芯片市场的份额降至 34%，大幅下滑，原因是美国出口管制限制了其产品供应，而以 Huawei 为首的本土竞争对手抢占了市场份额。中国芯片厂商正迅速填补受限 Nvidia GPU 留下的空白。

stories.content:
BEIJING (Oct 13): Nvidia's share of China's market for data-centre AI chips fell to 34% in the first half of 2026, as US export controls restricted supplies of its products and domestic rivals led by Huawei gained ground, according to an IDC report seen by Reuters.

Nvidia shipped 678,000 AI accelerators in China from January through June, down 44% from a year earlier, IDC data showed. AI accelerators are specialised chips used to train and run AI models.

Washington has restricted China's access to Nvidia's most powerful AI chips, limiting the range of products the US chipmaker can sell in the world's second-largest economy. Beijing, meanwhile, has promoted domestic alternatives and required Chinese companies to seek approval to import compliant Nvidia chips.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has repeatedly criticised Washington's export curbs, saying the policy forced a US company to cede China's $50 billion AI chip market to Huawei.

IDC did not specify which Nvidia products made up its 34% market share, or whether the figure included cutting-edge chips such as the B200 and B300, which are barred from export to China but have been smuggled into the country.

Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment.

Huawei shipped 572,000 AI accelerators, up from more than 300,000 a year earlier, giving it a 28% share of the overall market, IDC said.

Alibaba's chip-design unit T-Head held 7%, followed by Cambricon with 5%, Baidu's Kunlunxin with 4% and Hygon with 3%. Nine of the 11 Chinese chipmakers tracked by IDC increased shipments from a year earlier.

Total AI-accelerator shipments reached 2.008 million units in the first half. Shipments of graphics processing units, or GPUs — the chips most widely used to train AI models — fell 26% to 991,000 units, as supplies eligible for sale in mainland China remained limited, IDC said.

Shipments of other AI accelerators rose nearly 80% to 1.016 million units, overtaking GPUs by volume. This category includes chips designed for specific AI tasks, such as running trained models.

Huawei, T-Head, Kunlunxin and Cambricon together accounted for 95% of the non-GPU segment, which IDC said was being adopted by government agencies, internet companies and telecoms providers.

IDC said competition was shifting from the performance of a single chip to system-level capabilities, including how well chips work in a larger computing cluster.

IDC expects total accelerator shipments in China to grow 19% this year, even as GPU shipments fall 9%.

stories.content:
(Oct 13): A global slide in semiconductor stocks deepened, sending South Korea’s chip-heavy equity benchmark down 7% as concerns about AI overheating and Chinese competition intensified.

Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc shares dropped more than 8% each Tuesday, weighing on the Kospi. A gauge of Chinese technology stocks tumbled 3.6% before paring its drop, while Japanese flash memory firm Kioxia Holdings Corp shed more than 12%. US chipmakers slumped overnight.

Investor angst over the AI trade intensified after Broadcom Inc’s chief executive likened market sentiment to a casino and warned that financing the buildout will become a key problem. That further undermined the case for AI stocks, just as higher interest rates begin to take a toll on massive debt-funded deals and threaten once-hot initial public offerings.

“Uncertainty over whether the upcycle can last into 2028 and beyond appears to be weighing on valuations and share prices” of Korean chipmakers, said Ha SeokKeun, chief investment officer at Eugene Asset Management.

Korean stocks took the biggest hit, as investors also reacted to a report that Chinese rival CXMT Corp has made progress on a new memory architecture that Samsung and SK Hynix are also working on. The Seoul stock exchange briefly halted Kospi program trading for the first time since August.

The Kospi is now down a third from the record high it reached in June. The benchmark has fallen below its 200-day moving average. Foreigners have accelerated their exit, selling more than US$6.3 billion (RM25.7 billion) worth of Kospi shares on a net basis in October.

CXMT plans to roll out a new server-memory product by the end of 2026 that enables higher storage density, according to a report from *South China Morning Post* on Monday. That resurfaced fears of rapid development by Chinese chipmakers that have rattled global rivals this year.

“Samsung’s strong earnings have been overshadowed by concerns about future competition from CXMT and the sustainability of AI spending,” said Jung In Yun, chief executive officer at Fibonacci Asset Management Global. “These concerns may weigh on sentiment, but CXMT still needs to translate technological progress into commercially competitive production at scale.”

Broader worry over the longevity of the AI boom continues to weigh on industry stocks after last week’s collapse of a planned offering by Nvidia Corp-backed data centre company Firmus Grid Ltd.

Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said financing may be a bigger problem than chip shortages. “A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in,” the head of the American chipmaker said at an event in Singapore. They “set very extreme expectations only to find out that it’s almost like they are in a casino.”

This week’s earnings from ASML Holding NV and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co will help investors gauge how long bumper profit growth can last. Shares of TSMC, Asia’s most-valuable company, slipped as much as 2% Tuesday.

Record earnings from Samsung last week failed to give the stock a boost.

“Traders aren’t treating good news stories or lofty valuations as gospel any more, they’re digging much more carefully into the numbers and the underlying business case, with the whole AI trade still under the microscope,” said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade.

stories.content:
HONG KONG (Oct 13): Tencent Holdings is selling US dollar and offshore Chinese yuan, or dim sum, bonds in a deal that could raise at least US$4.5 billion as the Chinese technology giant seeks funding amid higher spending on artificial intelligence.

The sale comprises 10-year and 20-year US dollar notes and 10-year and 30-year offshore yuan notes, according to term sheets seen by *Reuters* on Tuesday, which did not specify the size of any tranche.

Tencent set initial guidance for the 10-year dollar notes at about 115 basis points over comparable US Treasury bonds. The 20-year notes were set at about 140 basis points over Treasuries, according to the sheets.

Order books for the two-tranche dollar offering topped US$2 billion, including US$525 million in interest from the joint lead managers, according to an updated message from the sheets.

The company set initial yield guidance at around 2.90% for the 10-year offshore yuan notes and 3.50% for the 30-year notes, the sheets showed.

Books for the 10-year and 30-year offshore yuan notes exceeded 35 billion yuan (US$5.2 billion), including 20.25 billion yuan in orders from the joint lead managers and 60 million yuan in additional proprietary interest, according to an updated message from the sheets.

On Monday, *Reuters* reported that Tencent was planning a dollar and offshore yuan bond sale that could raise at least US$4.5 billion.

Tencent did not immediately respond to a request seeking comment on Tuesday.

Tencent shares fell 1.3% on Tuesday, in line with the benchmark Hang Seng Index which was 1.1% lower, while outperforming the Hang Seng Tech Index, which dropped 2.7%. Tencent's shares have fallen about 30% so far this year.

The planned borrowing comes as Tencent increases investment in AI infrastructure and products.

Its capital expenditure more than doubled to 96.3 billion yuan in the first half of 2026 from 45.9 billion yuan a year earlier, according to its offering documents. The spending included computing equipment, software and data centres.

Technology companies have raised billions of dollars to finance AI investment, although investors have become more selective about companies funding costly AI infrastructure amid elevated borrowing costs.

Tencent last tapped the bond market in June, raising about US$4.66 billion through dollar- and yuan-denominated notes.

Tencent plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, according to the sheets.

The bonds are expected to be rated A1 by Moody's and A+ by S&P. Tencent is rated A1 by Moody's, A+ by S&P and A by Fitch, according to the term sheets.

JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, HSBC and Morgan Stanley are joint global coordinators for the dollar sale, the sheets showed.

ICBC (Asia), Agricultural Bank of China, Bank of China, Bank of Communications, China Construction Bank, Citic Securities, HSBC and JPMorgan are coordinating the offshore yuan sale, according to the sheet.

stories.title: Beijing Data Center Restrictions: Why In-City Capacity Is Scarce and What That Means for Deployments
stories.summary: Beijing's restrictions on data center construction have limited new capacity across the city's central districts for years, while energy-efficiency requirements for new and expanding facilities continue to tighten. The analysis explains how these policies create chronic scarcity of in-city capacity and shape deployment strategies for companies operating in the Chinese capital.
stories.why_it_matters: Scarcity in Beijing pushes workloads to surrounding Hebei and Inner Mongolia hubs and keeps pricing firm for licensed in-city capacity, benefiting incumbent operators. Multinationals and cloud providers must plan around regulatory access, not just cost or latency, when designing China deployments.
stories.title_zh: 北京数据中心限制:为何市内容量稀缺及其对部署的影响
stories.summary_zh: 北京市对数据中心建设的限制多年来一直制约着中心城区的新增容量，而新建及扩建设施的能效要求也在持续收紧。该分析解释了这些政策如何造成市内容量的长期稀缺，并影响在京企业的部署策略。
stories.why_zh: 北京的容量稀缺正把工作负载推向周边的河北和内蒙古枢纽，并使持牌市内容量的价格保持坚挺，令既有运营商受益。跨国公司和云服务商在规划中国部署时，必须围绕监管准入而非仅仅是成本或时延来设计方案。
stories.content:
Most data center markets in Asia are shaped by how fast capacity can be built. Beijing is shaped by where capacity is permitted to exist at all. Beijing data center restrictions have limited new construction across the city’s central districts for years, while energy-efficiency requirements for new and expanding facilities have tightened. For teams planning a deployment in the capital, that changes the question from which provider has the best site to which sites are available in the city in the first place.

## What restrictions have reshaped Beijing’s data center market?

Two policy directions, applied over several years, have reshaped supply. The first restricted new construction geographically. According to analysis by 451 Research, rules introduced in 2015 placed significant restrictions on new and expanded data center development in six central Beijing districts—Dongcheng, Xicheng, Chaoyang, Haidian, Fengtai, and Shijingshan. Efficiency requirements have also tightened over time. The PUE threshold applied to approved facilities moved from 1.5 to 1.4 in 2018 and later to 1.3, with new and expanding facilities assessed against it. The city also introduced energy-efficiency reviews and higher power tariffs for sites that fall short.

Together, these restrictions shape two local conditions that matter most. Opportunities for new development within the central districts are highly constrained, so expansion within the urban core is not simply a matter of cost or timing. Power is governed less by availability than by the efficiency standards a project must meet before approval. Neither restriction removes existing capacity, which is an important distinction when planning a site search.

## Where has new capacity gone instead?

Largely to the provinces around the capital, and further west. Hebei, Tianjin, and Inner Mongolia have absorbed much of the new supply serving Beijing demand, with cooler climates and lower power costs making it easier to meet efficiency requirements. The national “East Data West Computing” initiative, launched in 2022, formalized the broader pattern by encouraging data processing to move toward western provinces with abundant renewable generation, while keeping latency-sensitive services in the east. Carbon Brief’s explainer sets out how these policies fit together.

Water availability is another factor to consider when assessing cooling design in northern China, particularly for facilities supporting higher-density workloads. Buyers should examine both energy and water performance rather than assessing PUE in isolation. For a workload with no particular latency requirement, an out-of-city site can therefore be the more efficient and straightforward option. The trade-off is distance from users, networks, and staff.

## Which workloads still need to sit inside Beijing?

Fewer than teams often assume, but not none. The workloads that genuinely benefit from an in-city position tend to share a few characteristics: they serve users or counterparties concentrated in Beijing, depend on network proximity to carriers and exchange points in the city, or support business functions where staff need physical access at short notice.

Trading and payments systems, interactive platforms with a large Beijing user base, and front-end infrastructure for government-facing or enterprise-facing services commonly fall into this group. Batch processing, archival storage, model training, and most back-office systems usually do not. Many enterprises end up splitting the two, keeping a smaller in-city footprint for latency-sensitive and network-dependent components while placing bulk capacity in a neighboring province. That split works well when the network design between the two sites is planned deliberately rather than added afterward.

The growth of AI inference is also increasing demand for infrastructure closer to users and network traffic. Sometimes described as “AI factories” or “token factories”, these environments generate AI outputs continuously and can be sensitive to latency. For customers serving users in Beijing, PEK1’s access to the city’s network infrastructure may make it relevant for latency-sensitive inference deployments.

## Why does existing in-city capacity matter under Beijing’s restrictions?

Because comparable in-city capacity is difficult to replicate under current planning and efficiency constraints. In most markets, a provider’s position in a metro reflects investment decisions that a competitor could match given time and capital. In central Beijing, facilities inside the restricted districts generally predate the restrictions, which makes existing in-city capacity a structurally different proposition from capacity that is merely planned.

Digital Edge’s PEK1 sits in Chaoyang District, one of the six districts named in the 2015 rules, in a prime position on Beijing’s network infrastructure and within the city’s business district. The facility offers 8,361m² of colocation space across 1,801 cabinets, with 7.8MW of capacity, 4.4kVA per cabinet, 2N UPS redundancy, and a 100% dual power SLA. For buyers, the practical implication is that in-city options in Beijing should be evaluated on what is available now and how much room each site has to grow, rather than on a provider’s development pipeline. Our China data centers page sets out the facility in more detail.

## How do enterprises actually contract capacity in China?

Providing commercial data center and internet data center services in mainland China requires the relevant local licences. International customers therefore need to understand which licensed entity operates the facility and contracts for the services they use.

This is where our article on China disaster recovery becomes relevant. It makes the case for separating operators across primary and secondary sites, because an operator is a shared dependency: two facilities run by the same entity share regulatory and operational exposure as well as infrastructure. In China, acting on that means choosing among licensed local operators rather than among international providers, and understanding who actually runs each site on a shortlist. Anyone planning a second site will find the full argument there.

Digital Edge’s PEK1 operates through Chuanjun Information Technology, a fully licensed China operator, with bilingual support and local regulatory expertise alongside Digital Edge’s platform standards. For a wider view of when local hosting is necessary at all, and how cloud and colocation compare in this market, our China colocation guide covers the earlier stages of that decision.

## Which compliance signals are worth checking?

The ones that show a facility has been assessed against both local and international standards. In China, the two sit side by side, and a site that holds only one set tells an incomplete story.

On the local side, CQC certification against GB50174-2018 Level A covers data center design and construction under the Chinese national standard, and Cybersecurity Protection Level 3 reflects assessment under the country’s cybersecurity classification regime. On the international side, PEK1 holds ISO/IEC 27001 for information security management, together with ISO 9001, ISO 14001, ISO 14064, ISO 45001, and ISO 50001. Buyers should confirm that each certification remains current and understand whether it applies to the facility, the local operator or the wider Digital Edge platform.

For teams whose own reporting or audit obligations extend across markets, the useful question is whether a provider’s certification set is consistent across its footprint or assembled facility by facility. Consistency makes it easier to reuse evidence across markets rather than rebuilding it for each one.

## How does a Beijing deployment connect to the rest of Asia?

Beijing’s value to many architectures is as much about network position as floor space. The city is a dense carrier environment, and an in-city facility gives access to that ecosystem in a way an out-of-province site does not. Interconnection services within the facility handle connections between endpoints on site, which matters when a deployment spans several parties.

It is also worth being clear about which workloads need to be in mainland China at all. Regional services, aggregation layers, and capacity serving users across Asia often sit more naturally in Japan or South Korea, where Digital Edge operates facilities directly and where cross-border connectivity is more straightforward. A common pattern is a focused Beijing footprint for what must be in-country, with regional capacity elsewhere in Asia, connected deliberately rather than by default.

## Conclusion

Beijing data center restrictions have made site selection a question of both location and availability. The questions that matter are which facilities exist inside the restricted districts, how much capacity each has available, who holds the operating licence, and which parts of the workload genuinely need to be in the city rather than in a neighboring province.

For most enterprises, the answer is a smaller in-city footprint than first assumed, paired with capacity elsewhere and a network design that connects the two properly. Understanding the restrictions early helps teams plan around Beijing’s constraints, evaluate existing capacity realistically, and determine which workloads genuinely need an in-city deployment.

## Talk to Digital Edge

Digital Edge’s colocation services include PEK1 in Chaoyang District alongside facilities across Asia-Pacific — talk to our team about what a Beijing deployment would need and how it fits with capacity in the wider region.

stories.title: Carriers identify 200,000km subsea cable demand in GLF forecast
stories.summary: The Global Leaders Forum (GLF) has identified demand for over 200,000 kilometres of future subsea cable. This marks the industry's first aggregated carrier subsea forecast, compiled from a 12-month initiative.
stories.title_zh: GLF预测显示运营商海底光缆需求达20万公里
stories.content:
Carriers have identified demand for more than 200,000 kilometres of future subsea cable, according to findings published by the Global Leaders Forum (GLF) in a joint statement. This forecast is the industry's first aggregated carrier subsea forecast, developed after a 12-month initiative that brought together carriers and subsea vendors.The GLF stated that this figure demonstrates carriers continue to play a significant role in driving subsea investment alongside hyperscalers. The initiative addresses a fundamental gap in how carrier demand reaches the supply chain, as carriers serve a broad mix of customers including businesses and governments, making forecasting complex.Without better visibility of carrier requirements, the GLF warned that limited manufacturing and installation capacity risks disproportionate allocation. This could leave important connectivity needs underserved globally. To mitigate this, participating carriers submitted forward-looking project forecasts, which the GLF aggregated, anonymised, and consolidated into a single long-term industry forecast before sharing it with vendors.The GLF expects this forecast to help vendors plan production, allocate resources more efficiently, and deliver subsea infrastructure more flexibly. The organisation also highlighted rising demand, geopolitical uncertainty, regulatory complexity, and limited specialist manufacturing and installation capacity as key factors delaying subsea projects worldwide.Industry discussions at ITW Asia in January indicated delivery timelines have stretched to six years, with manufacturing backlogs reaching 150,000 kilometres. Around 100 new cable systems are currently competing for limited manufacturing capacity. Eduardo Mateo of NEC also pointed to permitting and vessel availability as critical bottlenecks beyond manufacturing.Enrico Bagnasco, chair of the GLF and CEO of Sparkle, emphasised that no single organisation can solve the subsea delivery challenge alone. He described the initiative as an important first step and stated that the GLF plans to continue engaging carriers and vendors regularly to share forward-looking insights responsibly.

stories.why_it_matters: A direct tie-up between a US frontier AI lab and Japan's largest IT services group would anchor one of Japan's biggest single data center investments and deepen Anthropic's infrastructure footprint beyond the US. stories.content:
NTT Data Group, a multinational IT services and consulting provider, is reportedly nearing an agreement with U.S. artificial intelligence company Anthropic to develop a large-scale data center in Osaka, in western Japan. According to a report from Nikkei Asia, the project would cost ¥1 trillion (US$ 6.3 billion) for construction with additional investment required for advanced servers and graphics processing units (GPUs).

While neither NTT Data, nor Anthropic have made any official statements about the project, Nikkei Asia reports that the facility is expected to have a power capacity of 500 MW, thus placing it among Japan’s largest data centers.

The companies are reportedly targeting to conclude negotiations by the end of NTT’s fiscal 2026, which ends in March 2027 and partial operations could begin by 2028. If completed, the facility would be Anthropic’s first dedicated data center in Japan. Neither NTT Data nor Anthropic commented on the reported negotiations.

Securing and obtaining 500 MW through the existing power grid remains a major challenge, prompting both companies to consider on site power generation and fuel cells as initial alternatives.

NTT Data operates facilities with a combined capacity exceeding 1,600 MW across not just Japan, but also other countries in APAC, and even has a presence in Latin America, as well as European markets like Germany, Netherlands, Spain, and the UK. The company has been expanding its capabilities in AI infrastructure, including facilities equipped with liquid-cooling technology.

A market report by Mordor Intelligence projects the Japanese data center market to increase from US$ 11.89 billion in 2026 to US$ 17.66 billion by 2030 with a 8.22 percent compound annual growth rate (CAGR) between 2026 and 2031 while power is expected to expand from 3.57 thousand MW to 11.17 thousand MW in the 2026 to 2031 forecast period at a CAGR of 25.62 percent.

stories.content:
CIMB, Credit Agricole CIB, DBS, Maybank, OCBC, Standard Chartered and UOB make up the consortium

\[SINGAPORE\] A consortium of seven lenders has arranged expanded multi-currency financing of RM15 billion (US$3.7 billion) for DayOne to support the continued development of its data centre platform in Johor, Malaysia.

CIMB, Credit Agricole CIB, DBS, Maybank, OCBC, Standard Chartered and UOB are the seven lenders involved in this facility, as mandated lead arrangers, bookrunners and joint co-ordinators.

The additional amount consists of a US$2.4 billion offshore term loan facility and a RM5.5 billion Murabahah facility.

Together with the RM15 billion multi-currency financing secured in 2025, the financing platform now stands at RM30 billion, a joint statement from the lenders noted on Tuesday (Oct 13).

The transaction “reinforces Malaysia’s position as a leading regional digital infrastructure hub”.

“Johor has attracted significant investment in data centre development, supported by its strong connectivity, robust infrastructure, access to skilled talent and proximity to regional markets,” it added.

Malaysia is on track to become one of Asia’s largest data centre markets. Its supply capacity is projected to record a nearly 39 per cent compound annual growth rate from 2023, to reach 4.2 to 6.1 gigawatts by 2030, based on Boston Consulting Group data.

This comes amid accelerating demand for cloud computing, artificial intelligence and digital services in the Asia-Pacific, such that developing scalable and resilient digital infrastructure is important to strengthen regional connectivity and economic growth.

Established in 2022, DayOne has expanded its footprint across Asia and Europe, in countries such as Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Finland and Spain.

The Singapore-headquartered firm most recently filed for a proposed Nasdaq initial public offering in the US on Oct 6, with plans to raise as much as US$5 billion, with a potential valuation of US$20 billion.

stories.title: SUBCO announces 850km Sydney-Melbourne fibre route
stories.summary: Australian network builder SUBCO has announced plans to build an 850km terrestrial fibre network connecting Sydney and Melbourne, adding a new high-capacity inter-capital route to its growing subsea infrastructure portfolio. The SM-1 network will have a minimum of 96 fibre pairs and is intended to provide direct connectivity between the two cities, which host the […]
stories.title_zh: SUBCO宣布建设850公里悉尼—墨尔本光纤线路
stories.content:
Australian network builder SUBCO has announced plans to build an 850km terrestrial fibre network connecting Sydney and Melbourne, adding a new high-capacity inter-capital route to its growing subsea infrastructure portfolio. The SM-1 network will have a minimum of 96 fibre pairs and is intended to provide direct connectivity between the two cities, which host the majority of Australia’s data centre and cloud infrastructure.

SUBCO said the route is being developed in response to increasing demand for low-latency, high-bandwidth connectivity between the Sydney and Melbourne markets, driven by hyperscale cloud infrastructure, AI workloads and enterprise data requirements.

The company said SM-1 will connect cable landing stations, carrier-neutral data centres and cloud on-ramps in both cities, providing an additional route between the markets and reducing reliance on existing inter-capital fibre networks. Survey notices have been issued and SUBCO expects to have the required permits in place, with construction commencing immediately. The company is targeting a Ready for Service date of June 2028.

Bevan Slattery, founder and co-CEO of SUBCO, said Sydney and Melbourne account for the “overwhelming majority” of Australia’s data centre capacity and cloud infrastructure, with demand for diverse connectivity expected to increase as AI and hyperscale workloads expand. “SM-1 gives our customers a purpose-built, high-capacity terrestrial path that complements our subsea network and ensures they have the infrastructure to scale without constraint,” he said.

The project adds a terrestrial component to SUBCO’s broader network expansion, which includes the 5,000km SMAP submarine cable linking Sydney, Melbourne, Adelaide and Perth. SMAP entered service in June with 16 fibre pairs and more than 400Tbps of capacity.

SUBCO is also developing the APX programme, a series of three subsea cable systems connecting Australia with Asia and the US. APX North is planned to run 9,500km from Sydney to Japan via Guam, while APX East-2 will span 10,000km between Guam and Los Angeles. APX West will cover 4,600km between Perth and Singapore, with branches to Jakarta and Batam. Each system is planned to have 24 fibre pairs, with SUBCO targeting completion of the three systems by 2029.

The APX systems are designed to add international route diversity and capacity as demand for connectivity between Australian data centre markets and overseas cloud and AI infrastructure grows.

Together with SMAP and SM-1, the projects will give SUBCO a network spanning international subsea routes and domestic inter-capital connectivity, linking Australian data centre markets with major connectivity hubs across the Indo-Pacific.

stories.title: Stepping out beyond Tokyo and Osaka
stories.summary: Japan's data center growth remains heavily concentrated in Greater Tokyo and Greater Osaka, which together account for 90% of the country's data center locations despite representing a small share of its land area. Industry voices are making the case for developing facilities in regional areas where land and power are more available.
stories.why_it_matters: Power constraints and disaster-resilience concerns in the two megaregions are pushing operators to evaluate secondary Japanese markets, which could reshape site selection and land pricing nationwide. Regional governments stand to gain investment, while developers face new challenges in connectivity and staffing outside the hubs.
stories.title_zh: 走出东京和大阪：日本数据中心向传统枢纽之外扩张
stories.summary_zh: 日本的数据中心增长仍高度集中于大东京和大阪地区，两地合计占全国数据中心选址的 90%，尽管其国土面积占比很小。业内人士正呼吁在土地和电力资源更充裕的地方区域开发设施。
stories.why_zh: 两大都市圈的电力限制和灾害韧性担忧正推动运营商评估日本的二级市场，这可能重塑全国范围内的选址逻辑和土地价格。地方政府有望获得投资，而开发商则需在枢纽之外应对网络连接和人才招聘方面的新挑战。
stories.content:
*There are strong compelling reasons for developing data centers outside of the traditional hubs of Tokyo and Osaka regions.*

The growth of data centers in Japan is highly concentrated in two regions – Greater Tokyo and Greater Osaka – together accounting for 90 per cent of data centre locations. Ironically, these two megaregions represent less than 10 per cent of the country’s land area, 40 per cent of the population, and half of the country’s total GDP of US$ 4.87 trillion.

Such hyper geographical concentration would have had catastrophic consequences if an earthquake happened. In seismic-prone Japan, such large-scale natural disasters are foreseeable risks. Hence, a diversification strategy away from those megacities is a natural step towards protecting and providing redundancies for these critical infrastructure.

Earthquakes and consequently higher seismic engineering premiums especially in densely populated megacities are just two risks that immediately come to mind – there are other equally compelling reasons for the move towards suburban corridors. Key among them are high capital investment required in Tokyo and Osaka compared to other regions in Japan. Land prices are much higher and availability is very limited in those two cities. According to a Mordor Intelligence report, average land prices in central Tokyo rose by an astounding 69 per cent in 2024, significantly raising the cost of development.

Also in densely built areas within the megaregions, large scale expansions are not practical. Japan has been ranked eighth globally on Cloudscene for data center density based on a population of 125.5 million.

Some areas also experience power supply constraints thus limiting buildouts.

The case for developing data centers in suburban areas gets even stronger when one takes into account community pushbacks. As with the rest of the data center hubs around the world especially in the US and Europe, community resistance is becoming a real risk. For example, the local community in Koto ward (Eastern Tokyo) was up in arms against data centers, according to Mordor report. This has pushed operators to develop in suburban areas like Inzai City which has rolled out the red carpet to data centers granting them municipal incentives. Inzai also has the advantage of having larger plots of land available for data centers. The number of data centers in the city now stands at 10, which is the largest after Tokyo and Osaka.

The other push factors towards a suburban setup is the extraordinary long wait time for grid connection approvals. Tokyo Electric Power Company reports a queue time of more than 36 months for over 10MW connections. As utilities balance renewable-generation integration with load growth, operators are resorting to paying extra upfront to secure provisional slots in the interim period.

Some developers have tried to solve this problem by installing on-site gas turbines and lithium-ion storage while waiting for utility supply but this only adds a layer of complexity and risk to the project.

### Government Initiatives

Acknowledging this, the government is actively promoting regional diversification of data centers.

Since 2021, the government has extended various types of assistance to companies developing data centers outside of the two mega regions and other metropolitan areas. The assistance includes resilience strengthening measures and communication efficiency. The government has also come up with initiatives such as “Regional Revitalization” and “Digital Infrastructure Development Plan 2030”, to promote regional diversification while also encouraging the decarbonisation of data centers.

Part of the initiatives include data center development through Watt-Bit collaboration where regional diversification is promoted through collaboration of power and telecommunications.

The government also hopes to create five or more data center hubs to enhance GX-driven industrial growth while regional DX promotion including AI utilisation is also encouraged.

The other policy relies on advanced technology to achieve low latency inter-data center connections using All Photonic Network technology by 2030 and advanced computing resource power load control by 2035. Lower latency and better connection would encourage data center development outside of the densely populated megaregions.

### Emerging DC clusters

One of the major players developing data centers outside of traditional hubs is SoftBank Group which is said to have identified Sakai City and Toyama as potential hubs for massive AI data centers and superclusters. Toyama (Nanto Campus) is emerging as a massive digital infrastructure hub due to its abundant power supplies (about 3.1GW) and its strategic location being part of an economic triangle with Tokyo and Osaka. One of the companies developing large-scale AI data centers there is Gigastream Toyama.

Hokkaido and Kyushu have also emerged as popular new data center clusters. Hokkaido (Sapporo and Ishikari) has the advantage of a cool climate supporting free air-cooling. Ishikari hosts major facilities, including Rakuten Ishikari data center and White Data Center (WDC) which makes use of winter snow for cooling.

Meanwhile, Kyushu, the most southerly island of Japan, stands out due to its many advantages such as abundant and affordable renewable energy, easy availability of land and power, direct submarine cable connections and its proximity to Shanghai and Seoul. The island has even been positioned as the data center gateway to East Asia.

As a result, hyperscalers and AI operators are rushing in to build, contributing to 88 per cent of all planned projects being self-built. Cumulative supply has risen exponentially from just 101 MW in 2023 to about 3 GW by Q2 2026, according to research firm DC Byte.

The island hosts some of the largest data centers in Japan, for example, IDC Frontier Asian Frontier and Telehouse Fukuoka, as well as Asia-Pacific Land’s upcoming Kitakyushu Data Center Campus, sited on 15.5 acres of land; and the US$ 2 billion Itoshima Campus, which aims to expand up to 150MW capacity.

Okinawa is an important landing point for submarine cables connecting Japan to North America and mainland Asia. Nagoya, an important industrial and manufacturing hub, meanwhile attracts data centers like KDDI/Telehouse and major network exchange hubs serving the Tokai and Kinki districts.

The subsidised 15MW AI data center in Fukushima is a clear example of the government’s commitment to distribute critical digital infrastructure nationwide.

According to <u>Data Center Map Japan directory,</u> as of  early June, there are a total of 256 data centers in Japan run by 73 operators. Out of that, 105 are in Tokyo and 55 in Osaka. This is followed by 10 in Inzai City, 9 in Yokohama, 8 in Sapporo and 6 each in Nagoya, Fukuoka and Kanazawa, 5 in Kawasaki, 4 each in Tsukuba, Naha, and Takamatsu,  and between 1 – 3 in a few other locations.

### Massive room for growth

Clearly, there is still a lot of room for growth in regions outside of Tokyo and Osaka. With compelling pull factors such as abundant renewable energy, lower costs, proximity to Tokyo and Osaka, or to manufacturing hubs, direct submarine cable connections and even free snow cooling, on the back of strong government support, it is only a matter of time before data center developers realise the advantages and start beating a path there.

However, relocating to suburban areas is not all smooth sailing. While land prices might be cheaper, the developer would have to fork out extra to invest in dark fiber routes and redundant substations. This will extend project timelines and costs thus affecting the overall data center supply market in Japan.

Still, data centers in non-traditional locations are perfect for edge and disaster-recovery workloads. More importantly, they possess a host of advantages as outlined earlier that their counterparts in the megacities do not have.

*\*This article has previously appeared in Issue 13 of cloud & datacenters magazine.*

stories.title: Global smartphone shipments record worst third quarter in 14 years amid memory shortage
stories.summary: ‘Challenging’ outlook for rest of 2026 as memory chip costs soar, says Counterpoint Research
stories.title_zh: 受memory芯片短缺影响，全球智能手机出货量创14年来最差第三季度
stories.content:
‘Challenging’ outlook for rest of 2026 as memory chip costs soar, says Counterpoint Research

\[BENGALURU\] Global smartphone shipments fell 20 per cent on the year to their lowest third-quarter level since 2012, as soaring memory chip costs and supply shortages pressured manufacturers and pushed up prices, preliminary estimates from Counterpoint Research showed on Monday (Oct 12).

Rising prices for memory components as artificial intelligence infrastructure projects corner supplies have driven up production costs and prompted manufacturers to raise retail prices, cut shipments and prioritise profitability over volumes.

“Consumers are holding on to their devices longer than estimated, increasingly considering refurbished devices and prioritising higher-value devices,” said Counterpoint senior analyst Shilpi Jain.

Samsung retained its top position with a 23 per cent market share, helped by demand for its Galaxy Z Fold8 series and stable component supplies for its mid-range devices. Shipments fell 3 per cent from a year earlier during the quarter.

Apple’s market share reached 22 per cent, crossing 20 per cent for the first time in a third quarter, despite a year-on-year decline in shipments.

The absence of a base iPhone 18 model resulted in a smaller launch-month channel fill than the full iPhone 17 lineup a year earlier, Counterpoint said.

Oppo and Vivo recorded shipment declines of more than 20 per cent. Xiaomi saw a more than 30 per cent fall, reducing its market share to 10 per cent as the company cut exposure to lower-priced devices and some overseas markets to protect margins.

“The outlook for the remainder of 2026 remains challenging,” Counterpoint said.

“Production cuts, tighter portfolios, and greater focus on premium devices are likely to continue, while price-sensitive segments face further pressure from higher device prices and limited availability of components.” REUTERS

stories.title: Trane launches LiquidStack CDU 2.X for AI data centres
stories.summary: Operators can now pre-order a cooling unit that aims to reduce redesigns as GPU roadmaps shift and rack densities for AI servers keep rising.
stories.title_zh: Trane推出面向AI数据中心的LiquidStack CDU 2.X液冷分配单元
stories.content:
Tue, 13th Oct 2026 (Today)
Trane Technologies has launched the LiquidStack CDU 2.X coolant distribution unit for AI data centres, designed to support current and emerging GPU platforms.

The product targets operators making cooling infrastructure decisions before finalising the computing hardware they will deploy, as rack densities rise and processor roadmaps continue to shift.

### Liquid cooling demand

Liquid cooling is becoming a greater focus for the data centre industry as AI workloads push heat loads in server racks beyond the range typically handled by conventional air cooling. In this context, coolant distribution units have become central to liquid-cooled system design because they manage the flow of coolant between facility water systems and IT equipment.

Trane says the CDU 2.X uses a common design intended to work across different AI silicon platforms, including current systems and forthcoming products such as NVIDIA Vera Rubin. The unit has flow capability of up to 3,750 litres per minute at 3.5 bar.

According to Trane, the new unit can be configured for end-of-row and rack-adjacent deployment. It also offers options for control valves, power feeds and redundancy arrangements, allowing operators to align installations with different facility layouts and resilience requirements.

### Flexible deployment

A key design goal is to limit the need for redesign when hardware plans change. That issue has become more pressing for data centre operators and developers that must commit to power and cooling infrastructure well before the final rack architecture is known.

Trane also says the CDU 2.X uses an ultra-low-harmonics variable frequency drive architecture designed to address harmonic distortion at the source. This can reduce the need for additional power-quality components and simplify system design.

Other specifications include support for facility inlet temperatures of up to 45C and lower approach temperatures, which Trane says can support efficient liquid cooling system layouts.

### Expanded portfolio

The launch expands Trane's broader liquid cooling portfolio under the LiquidStack brand. The company recently made its GigaModular CDU platform commercially available with an expanded capacity of 14 MW, broadening its offer for operators building high-density AI infrastructure.

Scott Smith, General Manager of LiquidStack at Trane Technologies, said the new system is intended to address the pace of change in AI infrastructure planning.

"Operators need cooling infrastructure that can adapt as GPU platforms and rack densities evolve," said Scott Smith, General Manager of LiquidStack at Trane Technologies.

"CDU 2.X combines the performance and flexibility customers need today with the headroom to prepare for what comes next, allowing them to configure cooling around their facility and deployment strategy rather than designing the facility around the CDU," added Smith.

The LiquidStack CDU 2.X is available for pre-order, with shipments due to begin in the second quarter of 2027.

stories.title: 'Wasting money, spending tokens': Companies still in search of AI use cases with worthwhile ROI, says Broadcom's Hock Tan
stories.summary: Both he and Intel CEO Tan Lip-Bu suggest that capital could be AI’s next biggest bottleneck
stories.title_zh: Broadcom的Hock Tan：企业仍在寻找具备可观ROI的AI用例，"浪费金钱、消耗token"
stories.content:
Both he and Intel CEO Tan Lip-Bu suggest that capital could be AI’s next biggest bottleneck

\[SINGAPORE\] Most companies are still trying to arrive at use cases for artificial intelligence (AI) that generate a return on investment, Broadcom’s CEO Hock Tan said on Monday (Oct 12).

While these companies have adopted AI in some form in their operations, their current use cases of generative AI are still “subtle” and are not necessarily raising productivity, he said in a panel discussion at a conference.

“Most companies out there cannot find any return on investment,” he said, adding that “people are just wasting money, spending tokens, trying to understand (AI)”.

He likened the situation to a child in a game arcade: “Ever thought when you’re a kid, you go to the arcade, your parents give you $10, you finish it in 10 minutes, and you haven’t learned anything? That’s what’s happening in enterprises today.”

He and Intel CEO Tan Lip-Bu were discussing the source of the next trillion dollars of investment in AI at DBS’ Asia Future Forward Conference, in a panel moderated by the bank’s CEO, Tan Su Shan.

Intel’s Tan said that investors are increasingly looking for a “real impact” from AI as they seek better returns on their investment, given the large amounts of capital that is being poured into the space.

## Capital crunch

The current AI boom is focused on the hardware providers, otherwise known as providers of the “picks and shovels”, said Broadcom’s Tan.

But the future value of AI is likely upstream, towards the builders of frontier models, who have the capability to disintermediate software players, he added.

“If there’re only picks and shovels, this phenomenon will not sustain,” he said. “What’s really driving this, or will sustain and grow this, is whether (tech companies) can build the frontier models that can create a lot of value.”

Hence, capital is likely the next bottleneck for the industry, with frontier models seeking the same sources of financing as the infrastructure players of today, he said.

Intel’s Tan said he expects AI to have an even bigger impact on the world than the Internet, with agents being able to improve efficiency, enabled by larger amounts of available data.

Despite fears that AI may be a bubble near its bursting point, the two chipmaker leaders do not see any signs of a slowdown in the sector, given the impact that AI can likely bring to humans.

Commenting on investors’ disappointment in OpenAI’s latest revenue forecast, Broadcom’s Tan noted that an annualised revenue of US$50 billion is “by itself, not that bad”, considering its status as a startup.

The disappointment investors feel stems from their not understanding the business model of such AI companies, which he said is viable “for now”.

“A lot of investors have no clue what they’re investing in, but set very extreme expectations,” he said. “It’s almost like they are in a casino, gambling.”

For now, these companies are losing money as they are spending heavily on training, but this might change with greater scale.

DBS’ Tan referred to the “token paradox”, the situation in which companies are burning more tokens than before, yet spending less. For example, DBS has quintupled its AI consumption, while managing to reduce overall token costs.

She said: “The next wave of winners … will be the enterprises that know how to adopt this for their own return on investments and return on equity.”

Speaking in a separate panel discussion on capital flows in the AI era, Franklin Templeton CEO Jenny Johnson said that nobody has really talked about the transformation that needs to happen in every industry because of AI technology.

“In the end, who cares about the picks and shovels of any of this? It’s all about what businesses are enabled for.”

stories.title: Nvidia opens up Vera Rubin rack and tray designs to OCP
stories.summary: Nvidia has contributed its Vera Rubin rack and tray designs to the Open Compute Project, with the new MGX 1.2 specification emphasizing liquid cooling for high-density AI systems. Opening the designs allows third-party manufacturers to build compatible infrastructure.
stories.why_it_matters: Standardizing next-generation rack designs through OCP accelerates the ecosystem of compatible cooling, power, and enclosure products, shortening deployment timelines for liquid-cooled AI facilities. For APAC data centre designers, it provides earlier visibility into the mechanical requirements of upcoming Nvidia platforms.
stories.title_zh: Nvidia向OCP开放Vera Rubin机架和托盘设计
stories.summary_zh: Nvidia 已将其 Vera Rubin 机架和托架设计贡献给 Open Compute Project，新的 MGX 1.2 规范重点强化了面向高密度 AI 系统的液冷支持。开放设计使第三方制造商能够构建兼容的基础设施。
stories.why_zh: 通过 OCP 标准化下一代机架设计，将加速兼容的散热、供电和机柜产品生态的形成，缩短液冷 AI 设施的部署周期。对亚太数据中心设计方而言，这使其能更早了解 Nvidia 未来平台的机电要求。
stories.content:
Nvidia is contributing its Vera Rubin rack and tray designs to the Open Compute Project (OCP), a move it claims will foster open standards.

Included in the tech giant’s infra gift are cable-and fan-free liquid-cooled compute trays, interoperable rack-scale interconnect infrastructure, and a liquid-cooled 5,000 amp busbar built for higher-power systems.

The Vera Rubin update ties to version 1.2 of its modular reference design standard, MGX. Opening up its infrastructure designs is not a new thing for Nvidia; it previously did the same with Blackwell. The standardization move lets manufacturers build around its platform, while keeping its compute hardware directly intertwined and therefore the center of attention.

This latest effort doubles down on liquid cooling, featuring connector solutions for inside trays that allow for cold plates to be swapped out more easily without any unwanted spillage. The MGX 1.2 spec also adds native 19-inch equipment support and higher-density rack designs, and supports rack deployments of up to 250 kilowatts.

“The bottleneck for AI factory buildouts is how fast we can manufacture and deploy,” Joe DeLaere, Nvidia’s product lead for AI infrastructure solutions, said during a press briefing. “So when the specification is open, the equipment makers and component developers can start fabricating right away and build a supply chain instead of waiting for a singular customer with one proprietary spec. So overall, that accelerates the entire industry. The ecosystem grows, and we grow with them.”

A separate spec extends the MGX beyond GPUs to cover the new Vera CPU rack, which Nvidia revealed has started shipping.

stories.title: Nvidia gears up to smash CPU hegemony as Vera starts shipping
stories.summary: Nvidia has begun shipping Vera, its dedicated discrete CPU platform designed to handle agentic AI workloads separately from its NVL72 systems. The architecture segregates CPU tasks to improve overall performance of large-scale AI deployments.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia's entry into standalone server CPUs directly challenges Intel and AMD in a segment they have dominated, and could reshape server procurement for AI facilities. Data centre designers should expect new rack-level architectures that pair discrete CPUs with GPU pods, affecting power and layout planning.
stories.title_zh: Vera开始出货，Nvidia准备打破CPU霸主地位
stories.summary_zh: Nvidia 已开始出货 Vera——其专用的独立 CPU 平台，旨在将 agentic AI 工作负载与 NVL72 系统分离处理。该架构通过隔离 CPU 任务来提升大规模 AI 部署的整体性能。
stories.why_zh: Nvidia 进入独立服务器 CPU 市场，直接挑战了 Intel 和 AMD 长期主导的细分领域，可能重塑 AI 设施的服务器采购格局。数据中心设计方应预期出现将独立 CPU 与 GPU 集群配对的新型机架级架构，这将影响供电与布局规划。
stories.content:
Nvidia’s Vera CPU offerings have commenced shipping in “multiple form factors,” the company confirmed.

Speaking ahead of the OCP Global Summit in San Jose, Joe DeLaere, Nvidia’s product lead for AI infrastructure solutions, said in a press briefing that dedicated Vera racks were “shipping now.”

The Vera CPU rack platform leans on Nvidia’s MGX modular reference architecture and acts as a dedicated side-cabinet for handling agentic workloads. The “discrete system” placed next to an NVL72, as DeLaere described it, is separated from the core Vera Rubin platform, as the CPUs in an NVL72 are “dealing with other types of orchestration management,” leaving not enough cores to perform tasks needed in agentic workflows.

DeLaere told press that Vera provides more than two-fold performance on agentic workloads compared to the previous Grace generation, measured using the SPEC CPU 2026 benchmark. He also cited 1.8-fold performance on Terminal Bench, which he described as measuring agent tasks involving real code running in real containers.

“If you get a Vera CPU rack, it's got over 20,000 cores available for agents to operate quickly and complete these tasks as fast as possible,” DeLaere explained during a briefing. “Because Vera CPU was designed specifically for agents with its high bandwidth and its high single-threaded performance, we see that it really accelerates the agentic tool calling and execution of code … and having those separate is really how we can achieve these tremendous agentic workload benchmarks.”

Nvidia has been gearing up to take on the CPU hegemony of AMD and Intel at a time when the demand for agentic workloads has shaken up the processor space, with Arm even breaking its long-standing licensing wheelhouse to launch physical chips.

Nvidia first announced plans for a standalone CPU business at the turn of the year, with the likes of Meta and CoreWeave among early customers. Amazon Web Services is also in line for Vera, with the hyperscaler billing it as an additional compute option for agentic workloads.

Vera entered full production in the spring, with it set to replace Grace as Nvidia’s flagship processor. It also marks somewhat of a departure from Nvidia’s traditional reliance on Arm designs for CPUs in that it features a core design developed largely in-house, though it does still use the Arm v9.2-A architecture.

In addition to availability as a standalone processor and a dedicated rack platform, Vera will also provide the CPU portion for the Vera Rubin Superchip, also set to release in the latter half of this year.

stories.title: SoftBank eyes possible AI data center project in Borneo
stories.summary: SoftBank is exploring a potential AI data center project in Borneo, partnering with tech company Grab and a government-owned oil and gas firm. The project would extend SoftBank's AI infrastructure ambitions into a region rich in energy resources but with limited existing data center capacity.
stories.why_it_matters: Pairing a tech investor with a ride-hailing platform and a state energy firm is an unusual consortium that could unlock power-secured sites outside saturated hubs like Johor and Jakarta. If it proceeds, Borneo would emerge as a new frontier market for AI infrastructure in Southeast Asia.
stories.title_zh: 软银考虑在婆罗洲建设AI数据中心项目
stories.summary_zh: SoftBank 正探讨在婆罗洲建设 AI 数据中心项目的可能性，合作方包括科技公司 Grab 和一家国有油气公司。该项目将把 SoftBank 的 AI 基础设施雄心延伸至能源资源丰富但现有数据中心容量有限的地区。
stories.why_zh: 科技投资方、出行平台与国有能源公司组成的是一个不同寻常的联合体，可能解锁柔佛、雅加达等饱和枢纽之外电力有保障的选址。若项目落地，婆罗洲将成为东南亚 AI 基础设施的新兴前沿市场。
stories.content:
SoftBank is partnering with Singaporean tech company Grab and a Malaysian oil and gas firm for a potential AI data center project in Borneo.

SoftBank Group, Grab Holdings, and Petroleum Sarawak Berhad (Petros) signed a framework agreement this month to explore the development of an artificial intelligence (AI) and digital infrastructure platform in Sarawak, Malaysia.

Full details of any planned data center development weren’t shared.

Under the agreement, the three parties will “collaborate to develop a roadmap” for the phased development of the platform, which will “support Sarawak’s ambition to develop a high-value, technology-driven economy, while contributing to the expansion of Malaysia’s digital infrastructure and connectivity.”

The companies said the collaboration will also “explore opportunities across the wider AI value chain,” including AI compute and services, advanced technologies, robotics, local workforce, and community development.

Petros is a state-owned oil and gas firm established and wholly owned by the Government of Sarawak.

Founded as MyTeksi in 2012, Nasdaq-listed Grab offers a so-called ‘super-app’ across Asia offering ride-hailing, food delivery, and digital payment services on mobile devices. The company is a major AWS customer.

Sarawak is a Malaysian state located on the island of Borneo. Not known as a major data center hub, several planned projects have been announced there in recent years.

Poseidon Technologies is planning a facility on the island, announced in October 2023. Aizo Group and Netrunner announced plans for a data center in Sarawak in October 2024.FutureData is targeting a 500MW project there.

stories.title: Microsoft's senior director of AI systems hardware architecture joins OpenAI
stories.summary: Wilson Vu to work on OpenAI's compute architecture
stories.title_zh: 微软AI系统硬件架构高级总监加入OpenAI
stories.content:
The senior director of hardware architecture, AI systems, at Microsoft has left for OpenAI.

Wilson Vu worked for Microsoft for 12 years, across three stints at the tech giant. He most recently ran a team developing AI and GPU platforms.

He will now work on compute architecture as a member of the technical staff at the generative AI firm.

Vu has also worked as a hardware engineer on AI systems and accelerated platforms at Meta, a systems design lead at Salesforce, a hardware development engineer at Supermicro, and a principal engineering manager at GoDaddy.

OpenAI is developing its own AI hardware to support a growing compute fleet, which includes Nvidia and AMD GPUs, Google TPUs, and its own Jalapeño chips.

Jalapeño is expected to be deployed in limited quantities later this year, and more widely deployed next year.

stories.title_zh: 微软公布Azure Maia 300 AI加速器架构细节
stories.summary_zh: Microsoft 公布了其 Azure Maia 300 AI 加速器的架构细节，并表示将从 2027 年起大规模部署这款自研芯片，使其成为其全线产品 AI 工作负载的主要硬件。此举旨在降低公司对 Nvidia GPU 的依赖。
stories.why_zh: 又一家 hyperscaler 将核心 AI 工作负载交给自研芯片，加剧了对 Nvidia 数据中心业务的压力，也验证了 Google 和 Amazon 所走的自研芯片路线。对亚太 colocation 和云计算市场而言，这预示着新建项目中硬件部署将更加多元化，功率密度要求也将发生变化。
stories.content:
Microsoft has introduced the Azure Maia 300, its third-generation AI accelerator, as a complete system for cloud-scale agentic inference. The architecture co-designs software, silicon, physical rack infrastructure, networking, and data centers.The Maia 300 is engineered to sustain locality, provide sufficient memory capacity and bandwidth, and minimize data movement. It also aims to scale communication efficiently within a data center's fixed power and cooling envelopes.
### Architectural Innovations

The Maia 300 evolves the Software Defined Locally Accessed Dataflow Architecture (SDLA) for long-context, reasoning-intensive, and decode-heavy inference. Its multi-chiplet architecture places compute on TSMC N2P for performance-per-watt benefits, while memory controller and I/O functions use optimized dies.This design increases compute FLOPs by 36 per cent, adds 2.5 times HBM bandwidth, and provides 14 per cent more scale-up bandwidth. The system also introduces enhanced MXFP4 and sub-3-bit storage formats for optimized low-precision inference.These narrower representations reduce memory footprint and data movement. This allows the system to support larger models, longer contexts, and more concurrent sessions within the same power envelope. The memory hierarchy combines software-managed on-die SRAM with eight HBM4 stacks, offering 288 GB of capacity and 18 TB/s of bandwidth per accelerator.
### Network and Rack Design

Maia 300 integrates a one-scale-up fabric from pod to superpod, supporting up to 12,288 accelerators with custom AI transport based on Ethernet. This two-tier network builds a high-performance superpod. The system presents one communication model to software, enabling direct data movement to any accelerator within a superpod.The rack-scale architecture integrates 96 accelerators across 24 four-accelerator trays within a 167 kW rack, doubling the accelerator density of Maia 200. Liquid cooling removes over 80 per cent of the rack's thermal load from accelerators, voltage regulators, and switch ASICs.Rack and row-level power telemetry connect with data center operations. This enables dynamic power allocation and workload optimization. Maia 300 delivers up to 7 times greater rack-scale token throughput and more than 2.5 times the performance per watt compared with Maia 200.

stories.title: iCents Group Bags RM21 Mil Job From US-Based Company for EPCC Works in Selangor
stories.summary: Cleanroom services provider iCents Group Holdings Bhd (KL:ICENTS) said it has secured a contract worth RM21.05 million to undertake engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning (EPCC) works for the turnkey development of a semiconductor wafer processing facility in Selangor.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.title_zh: iCents Group获美国公司2100万令吉合同,在雪兰莪承建半导体晶圆厂EPCC工程
stories.content:
*This article has been amended for accuracy*

KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 12): Cleanroom services provider iCents Group Holdings Bhd (KL:ICENTS) said it has secured a contract worth RM21.05 million to undertake engineering, procurement, construction and commissioning (EPCC) works for the turnkey development of a semiconductor wafer processing facility in Selangor.

The contract was awarded by a Malaysian subsidiary of a US-based company, iCents said in a bourse filing on Monday, without identifying the company.

“This contract represents another meaningful step in strengthening our participation within the semiconductor industry,” iCents managing director Vincent Ong Mum Fei said in a statement.

The semiconductor wafer processing facility will be built in four phases.

Phase 1 is worth RM36.15 million and comprises two stages. The first stage, worth RM21.05 million, has been awarded and is expected to be completed within 18 weeks. The second stage, worth RM15.10 million, iCents said in a statement has been identified in the letter of award but has yet to be formally awarded.

iCents said the project is expected to contribute positively to its earnings and net assets for the financial year ending June 30, 2027 onwards until the project’s completion.

Looking ahead, the group said it remains focused on strengthening its position in high-specification industries, particularly semiconductors, data centres, pharmaceuticals and advanced manufacturing. It will continue to pursue opportunities in Malaysia and selectively expand its regional presence in Thailand and Indonesia.

iCents shares closed 1.5 sen or 1.75% lower at 83.5 sen, valuing the group at RM417.5 million.

stories.title: DBS CEO Tan Su Shan says market is repricing AI financing risks
stories.summary: She notes that weaker firms may see their credit ratings revised downwards
stories.title_zh: 星展银行CEO陈淑珊：市场正在重新定价AI融资风险
stories.content:
She notes that weaker firms may see their credit ratings revised downwards

\[SINGAPORE\] The market is repricing the risks around investments related to the buildup of artificial intelligence that could lead to more discipline in financing, according to DBS chief executive officer Tan Su Shan.

“The market has spoken,” Tan said in an interview with Bloomberg Television on Monday (Oct 12).

“It’s not a bad thing because now, people are asking for higher returns, and people are also looking at structures."

“They’re making sure that whatever money is now being hoovered into the whole AI capex ecosystem will lead to some kind of long-term ROI that can then be repaid back to debt or bond or equity holders.”

Tan, who leads South-east Asia’s biggest lender, said weaker firms may see their credit ratings revised downwards, though this risk repricing is “healthy” as the market wants to make sure that big financial commitments are sustainable.

DBS has originated about S$25 billion or US$20 billion of AI deals in 2026 so far, often as lead manager on syndicated loans and has held only a fraction of that, Tan said. The financing is mostly for hardware, from semiconductors and memory chips to data centres, she added. BLOOMBERG
